title: He has filled the hungry (Luke 1:39–56)
hookLine: Mary's song turns the world upside down, and Luke's whole gospel will follow it

cards: Mary doesn't stay home with her news. Luke says she went with haste into the hill country of Judah, to the house of Zechariah, to see Elisabeth, the sign the angel gave her.
A young woman, newly pregnant, and an older relative, the one people called barren, now six months along. Two unlikely mothers under one roof.
Mary steps through the door and greets her, and the baby inside Elisabeth jumps. Luke says the babe leaped in her womb. Some readers say John, not yet born, is already doing his job: pointing.

teach.b: Elisabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries out: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." And then Mary sings.
In the King James Bible: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In Latin the first word is Magnificat, and that's the song's name.
It starts personal: God has looked on me, a lowly servant.

teach.h: THE MIGHTY DOWN, THE LOWLY UP.
teach.b: Then it widens and turns the world upside down: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away."
Mary sings it in the past tense, as if it's already happened. It echoes an older song, sung by Hannah in the book of Samuel, another woman who praised God for a child and a world turned over.
Luke puts it at the start because his whole Gospel follows this song. Again and again, the poor are lifted and the comfortable unsettled.

teach.h: HE HATH FILLED THE HUNGRY WITH GOOD THINGS.
teach.b: Later, in Luke's version of his sermon, Jesus says: "Blessed are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled." Mary's song is the overture, and the rest of the book plays its tune.
Catholic Vespers and Anglican Evensong still sing or say it each evening. Some hear it mostly as God's mercy to the humble heart; others also hear a call to feed the hungry, here and now.

how: The Magnificat is sung or said daily in several traditions: at Vespers in the Catholic Church, at Evening Prayer or Evensong in Anglican churches, and at the morning service in Orthodox churches; some Christians also connect it with feeding the hungry.

games.q: you're Mary, newly pregnant, with news no one will believe. where do you go?
o: stay home and tell no one.
go with haste to Elisabeth in the hill country.
games.why: she hurries to Elisabeth, the sign the angel gave her. the baby leaps, Elisabeth blesses her, and Mary sings.

practice: Think of where hunger is close to you: a neighbor living alone, a food bank in your town, a coworker who's broke until payday, someone on the corner you pass every day.

Picture one face, and a plate set in front of them, not scraps, good things, the way Mary sang it. If you pray, offer that picture to God as part of Mary's song; if not, let it shape one real thing you'll do.

wordCard.voice: Magnificat, the name of Mary's song, from its first Latin word, magnify: she sings that God lifts the lowly and fills the hungry with good things.

orig.note: Greek: makes great, magnifies. the first word of Mary's song; in Latin, Magnificat.

carryVoice: Your line: the hungry filled. Mary's song, still sung as the day ends. Until tomorrow.
